content: Non-English publications were included in the review process. Systematic evidence reviews were conducted following the methodologies outlined in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) Methods Manual. These reviews adhered to Cochrane and AHRQ standards for systematic searches, risk of bias assessments, and treatment effect estimations. Data from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were pooled for meta-analyses when appropriate or summarized narratively when pooling was deemed unsuitable by the review team. Each systematic review team developed a detailed protocol outlining their planned methods for literature searching, including databases searched, time periods covered, search strategies, trial selection, data extraction, risk of bias appraisal, and data synthesis and reporting. These protocols were reviewed and edited by the WHO Technical Unit, an independent methodologist, and shared with the Guideline Development Group (GDG) for feedback before being finalized and published in an open-access repository. For each intervention, the systematic review teams created structured evidence syntheses for each outcome at pre-specified time points, by comparator, and included subgroup analyses. These were presented in a Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations (GRADE) evidence profile format. The GRADE system was used to assess the certainty of the evidence for specific outcomes of interventions in populations or subpopulations. Certainty was graded as high, moderate, low, or very low based on five criteria. The GDG determined the overall certainty of evidence across all critical outcomes for each recommendation, which could differ from the systematic review team's assessment. In cases of consistent benefit or no difference across outcomes, the highest certainty rating was applied. Conversely, inconsistency in estimates led to the lowest certainty rating being applied. When critical outcomes were sufficient to support a recommendation, the highest certainty rating was selected, provided the recommendation remained unchanged even if other critical outcomes had lower certainty. Evidence and recommendations for each intervention included an evaluation of benefits, harms, and the certainty of evidence. The WHO guideline for the non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain (CPLBP) in adults in primary and community care settings also included a qualitative evidence synthesis focusing on older adults. This synthesis aimed to provide the GDG with insights into the values, preferences, resource implications, equity, acceptability, and feasibility of interventions from the perspective of older adults and their caregivers. The synthesis followed the Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care (EPOC) protocol and review template. Recommendations were formulated using the GRADE Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) framework for public health interventions. Before proposing draft recommendations, the GDG reviewed EtD summary documents for each intervention, which included GRADE evidence profile tables and qualitative evidence on values, preferences, resource implications, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. These judgments were informed by the GDG members' expertise, knowledge, and observations, as well as qualitative evidence synthesis where available. The GDG used a consensus-based process to determine whether to make a recommendation, its direction, and its strength. Consensus was defined as agreement or acceptance by a pre-specified threshold of GDG members, allowing for minor disagreements. Principles and thresholds for decision-making were established at the beginning of the second GDG meeting series. A quorum of at least two-thirds of GDG members was required for any recommendation proposal, with at least 60% agreement needed to formulate a recommendation and 70% agreement required for strong recommendations. Strong recommendations were made when there was moderate or high certainty evidence supporting a favorable balance of benefits over harms (or vice versa) and when interventions were judged to be highly acceptable, feasible, equitable, and valued by people with CPLBP. Conditional recommendations were made when overall certainty was low or very low, or when judgments in other domains indicated variability or uncertainty. The guideline development process included multiple rounds of review and revision. Following the third GDG meeting in December 2022, a draft guideline document was prepared and circulated for feedback. The revised document was reviewed by the GDG, Steering Group, and external peer reviewers before final approval by the WHO Guideline Review Committee in June 2023. Subsequent modifications were limited to factual corrections and language improvements for clarity and adherence to WHO style. The guideline emphasizes holistic, person-centered, equitable, non-stigmatizing, and integrated care for adults with CPLBP. It recognizes the biopsychosocial nature of CPLBP, which occurs within personal and social contexts influenced by culture, beliefs, expectations, history, environment, gender, age, and socioeconomic status. Care should be tailored to these determinants and delivered in a way that avoids stigmatization, focuses on functional goals, and supports participation in valued life activities. Equity in care is a guiding principle, ensuring that all individuals with CPLBP receive care regardless of age, gender, socioeconomic status, ethnicity, or other factors. The guideline acknowledges the role of social and structural determinants, such as stigma, discrimination, and inequities, in shaping pain experiences and access to care. Integrated and coordinated care is essential, particularly for older adults and those with comorbid conditions. Care should be accessible across health and social systems, coordinated among multidisciplinary health workers, and involve active participation from individuals in developing their care plans.
